edges.description: Confirms TRPV4-mediated calcium influx is required for normal osteoclast terminal differentiation and resorptive activity, but does not model the ANFH2 disease direction: the knockout produces the opposite phenotype (reduced resorption, increased bone mass) to what the gain-of-function hypothesis for ANFH2 predicts (excess resorption, bone loss). No gain-of-function knock-in model exists for this variant or an equivalent one.
edges.limitations: Opposite-direction genetic perturbation: a null allele cannot demonstrate that a constitutively active channel drives excess resorption, only that channel activity is required for normal resorption. The inference to ANFH2's gain-of-function direction is by analogy, not direct evidence.

nodes.description: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head is characterized by compromised blood flow to the femoral head, with microvascular thrombosis a common finding across non-traumatic osteonecrosis generally. The femoral head is anatomically vulnerable because it lacks collateral blood vessels and is a constantly weight-bearing, mechanically stressed joint - features the authors propose synergize with systemic TRPV4 gain-of-function activation to produce localized ischemia.

nodes.description: Optical recording of TRPV4 Ca2+ "sparklets" (local, quantal fluorescence transients representing single-channel openings within a cluster) shows markedly increased channel activity per site in both proband-derived dermal fibroblasts and mutant-TRPV4-transduced HEK293 cells compared with controls, without an increase in the number of channels per site - confirming the calcium overload is driven by longer channel open times.

nodes.description: TRPV4 mediates basolateral Ca2+ influx specifically in large osteoclasts once RANKL-evoked Ca2+ oscillations decline, sustaining the NFATc1-dependent gene transcription required for terminal differentiation and resorptive activity. Genetic ablation of Trpv4 in mice increases bone mass by impairing bone resorption, indicating that TRPV4 signaling normally promotes osteoclast differentiation and resorption. This evidence is from the opposite (loss-of-function) direction: no study has directly measured osteoclast activity in cells carrying the ANFH2 gain-of-function variant, so the inference that excess TRPV4 activity would drive excess resorption is proposed by analogy rather than demonstrated.

nodes.description: Bilateral avascular necrosis of the femoral head, typically diagnosed by hip radiography and MRI (the gold standard), staged using the Steinberg classification. In the founding family, all four affected siblings had bilateral hip involvement, compared with about two-thirds of a sporadic (non-TRPV4) osteonecrosis comparison cohort, and had already reached Steinberg Stage III-V (subchondral fracture through end-stage secondary arthritic change) by the time of diagnosis. The other two clinically recognized TRPV4-opathy phenotype categories (skeletal dysplasia, peripheral neuropathy) and a primary coagulopathy were each specifically examined for and excluded in this family, supporting ANFH2 as a distinct TRPV4-related entity rather than an atypical presentation of one of those.

The femoral head's lack of collateral blood supply is the anatomical reason this specific site is vulnerable to fracture once ischemic.

nodes.description: A c.2480_2483delCCCG frameshift deletion followed by a c.2486T>A substitution in the last exon of TRPV4 truncates the 871-amino-acid channel protein (p.V829Wfs*3), eliminating a highly conserved C-terminal region that includes residues within a calmodulin-binding domain. Unlike previously characterized TRPV4 C-terminal truncations, which cause loss of channel activity, this variant produces a gain of function: functional measurements in patient-derived dermal fibroblasts and stably transduced HEK293 cells show markedly increased TRPV4 activity, caused specifically by longer channel open times rather than an increase in the number of channels per site.

nodes.description: The authors propose that TRPV4 gain-of-function calcium overload in vascular endothelium, acting together with the mechanical stress of weight-bearing at the hip, causes endothelial dysfunction and vasoconstriction. TRPV4 is expressed in vascular endothelium, where it normally regulates vasodilation and vascular tone, and TRPV4-mediated vasoconstriction (via COX-dependent prostanoid production and thromboxane receptor potentiation) has been demonstrated elsewhere in the vascular endothelium. This step is explicitly framed by the authors as a proposed, not directly demonstrated, mechanism for this disease.
